What does a jupyter notebook do? 
Pondered
 · 
15s
 · 
15s
A Jupyter Notebook is an interactive, web-based document that combines:
Live code execution
 — You write code in cells and run them one at a time, seeing output immediately
Narrative text
 — Markdown cells for explanations, documentation, and commentary
Rich output
 — Tables, charts, plots, images, and even interactive widgets inline alongside the code
Key Characteristics
Cell-based
 — Content is organized into cells (code cells or markdown cells) that can be run independently or all together
Kernel-backed
 — A language "kernel" (commonly Python, but also R, Julia, etc.) runs the code behind the scenes and maintains state between cell executions
Stateful
 — Variables and data persist across cells — you can define a variable in one cell and use it in the next
.ipynb
 format
 — Notebooks are stored as JSON files with the 
.ipynb
 extension, embedding code, output, and metadata together
Common Use Cases
Data science & analysis
 — Exploring datasets, cleaning data, building models
Education
 — Teaching programming with a mix of explanation and runnable examples
Prototyping
 — Quick experimentation with ideas before turning them into scripts
Reports
 — Sharing reproducible analyses with narrative, code, and results in one document
The name "Jupyter" comes from 
Ju
lia, 
Pyt
hon, and 
R
 — the three languages it originally supported, though it now works with many more.

Claude Code's 
NotebookEdit
 tool is used specifically for working with Jupyter notebooks in a more structured way. Here's what it does:
Core Use Cases
1. Cell-level editing without JSON wrangling
Instead of manually parsing and modifying the 
.ipynb
 JSON structure, 
NotebookEdit
 understands notebooks natively. You can tell it:
"Insert a new cell after cell 3 with this code"
"Replace cell 5's content with this markdown"
"Delete cell 2"
2. Three edit modes
Insert
 — Add a new cell at a specific position
Replace
 — Swap out a cell's content
Delete
 — Remove a cell entirely
3. Cell type awareness
You specify whether a cell is a 
code
 cell or a 
markdown
 cell, and the tool handles the formatting correctly.
Why It Exists
The practical problem it solves: 
.ipynb
 files are complex JSON with nested structures (
cells
, 
source
, 
metadata
, 
outputs
, 
execution_count
, etc.). Editing them with a plain text tool means:
Risk of breaking the JSON structure
Difficulty targeting one cell among many
Managing line-by-line source arrays (Jupyter stores cell content as arrays of strings)
NotebookEdit
 abstracts all that away, so Claude Code can manipulate notebooks at the cell level cleanly.
Realistic Scenarios
A data scientist asks Claude to 
"add a cell that loads the CSV and shows the first 5 rows"
"Add a markdown cell explaining what the next code block does"
"Remove the broken cell and replace it with a fixed version"
Without it, you'd do the same work — just with more manual JSON editing, which is what I'd do in this environment.
